# The Far Future of Cosmology in an Accelerating Universe

As the standard ΛCDM model of cosmology is extrapolated into the far future, it reveals a startling and profound implication: the very evidence that allows us today to understand the universe's origin and evolution will eventually disappear entirely. This is not a matter of technological limitation or observational difficulty—it is a fundamental consequence of the accelerating expansion driven by dark energy, which will progressively erase the observable signatures of our cosmic history.

## The Vanishing of Hubble Expansion

In the current epoch, we detect the expansion of the universe through the redshift of distant galaxies—a direct observational consequence of Hubble's law. However, as cosmic acceleration continues unabated, driven by the cosmological constant (Λ), distant galaxies will eventually recede beyond our cosmological horizon. Over sufficiently long timescales—on the order of hundreds of billions to trillions of years—every galaxy outside our Local Group will red-shift beyond detectability and cross the horizon, disappearing from view permanently. The Local Group itself will have merged into a single galaxy, gravitationally bound and immune to the Hubble flow. What remains will be an isolated "island universe": a solitary galactic remnant surrounded by an empty, dark void, with no other galaxies visible against the black backdrop of space.

## Fundamental Epistemological Limits for Future Observers

This transformation carries a striking implication for the observers who might inhabit this future universe. Astronomers in this era—whether human descendants or other intelligent beings—will face a fundamental epistemological barrier. Unlike scientists today, who can observe the expansion of space and trace the history of the universe back to the Big Bang, these future observers will find themselves confronted with a static-seeming island of stars and stellar remnants, with no empirical means of inferring that the universe is expanding, that it originated from a hot dense state, or that it once contained countless other galaxies. They will be unable to reconstruct the cosmological narrative that we currently take for granted, not due to any failure of scientific method, but because the physical evidence itself will have become permanently inaccessible.

## The Loss of Cosmology's Key Empirical Pillars

This epistemological crisis stems from the disappearance of three foundational pillars of modern cosmological evidence:

**Vacuum Energy and Cosmic Acceleration**: While dark energy will remain dynamically dominant, its primary observational signature—the accelerating recession of distant galaxies—will no longer be detectable, since there will be no distant galaxies left to observe. The very mechanism driving cosmic evolution will become empirically invisible.

**The Cosmic Microwave Background**: The CMB, our most direct relic of the early universe, will have redshifted into oblivion. Its photons will be stretched to wavelengths so extreme, and its energy density diluted to such a degree, that it will become utterly undetectable, drowned below the noise floor of any conceivable instrument. This "smoking gun" of the Big Bang—perhaps the single most compelling piece of evidence for the hot early universe—will effectively cease to exist as an observable phenomenon.

**Primordial Nucleosynthesis**: The relative abundances of light elements (hydrogen, helium, lithium) that provide crucial evidence for Big Bang nucleosynthesis will become obscured. Over cosmic timescales of this magnitude, successive generations of stellar processing will have thoroughly reprocessed the primordial material, erasing the pristine abundance ratios that currently allow us to confirm predictions of early-universe physics.

## The End of Empirical Cosmology

The cumulative loss of these three pillars represents more than an inconvenience for future scientists—it signifies the effective termination of empirical cosmology as a viable scientific discipline. Cosmology as we practice it today relies fundamentally on being able to observe direct physical evidence of the universe's dynamic history: its expansion, its thermal past, and its primordial composition. When all three lines of evidence vanish simultaneously, future civilizations will lack any observational foothold from which to deduce that the universe is anything other than a static, eternal, and unchanging island of matter. The scientific method, however rigorously applied, cannot recover information that has been permanently erased by the physics of cosmic expansion.

## An Ironic Return to a Static Universe

Perhaps the most striking aspect of this scenario is its historical resonance. The universe in this far future state will appear observationally static to its inhabitants—eternal and unchanging, with no evidence of a beginning or of large-scale motion. This mirrors, with poignant irony, the original mathematical description of the de Sitter universe, first formulated using static coordinates that depicted an unchanging, eternal cosmos. Just as early 20th-century cosmologists initially conceived of the de Sitter solution in a static form—only later reinterpreting it in terms of an expanding spacetime—future observers, situated within a universe genuinely dominated by dark energy, will find themselves inhabiting what appears to be that very static picture. The mathematical fiction of the past will become the observational reality of the future, closing a strange loop in the conceptual history of cosmology: what began as a static model later understood to be dynamic will end as a dynamic universe that appears, to those living within it, irreducibly static.

Modern cosmology stands on remarkably solid observational footing. Over the past few decades, converging lines of evidence—the cosmic microwave background radiation, the abundances of light elements produced during Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the large-scale distribution of galaxies, and the accelerating expansion revealed by distant supernovae—have established the ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter) model as the standard framework for understanding our universe's history and evolution. This model posits a universe approximately 13.8 billion years old, having expanded from an extraordinarily hot, dense initial state, and currently undergoing accelerated expansion driven by a cosmological constant (Λ), or dark energy.

While considerable effort has been devoted to understanding the universe's past and present, this paper takes a different approach: we extrapolate the ΛCDM model forward in time, asking what observers in the distant future will actually be able to detect and infer about cosmology. This is not merely an academic exercise—it carries profound implications for the epistemological status of cosmology as a science and raises deep questions about the nature of scientific knowledge itself when crucial observational evidence becomes permanently inaccessible.

The ΛCDM model, validated extensively by current observations, makes definite predictions about the future evolution of the universe. 4. **The gravitational unbinding and evaporation of structures**: Galaxy clusters will evaporate through gravitational scattering processes, and eventually even structures like the Local Group will be affected by the relentless dilution imposed by dark energy.

We term the resulting future state an "island universe" scenario, harkening back to early 20th-century debates about whether galaxies were "island universes" unto themselves. In the far future, our Local Group (or whatever gravitationally bound remnant persists) will find itself effectively isolated—surrounded by an apparently empty, static void, with no other galaxies visible within the observable horizon.

Once no such standard candles remain observable (because no external galaxies exist within the horizon), this diagnostic tool is lost entirely. Ironically, the very physics responsible for creating this future isolated state will itself become unknowable to observers embedded within it.

When de Sitter first proposed his solution to Einstein's field equations in 1917, he employed a static coordinate patch that made the spacetime appear time-independent and spatially bounded by a horizon—a description that seemed to conflict with the later-recognized expanding nature of the same spacetime when expressed in different coordinates (e.g., the flat FLRW-like coordinates now standard in cosmology).

We show that this apparent conflict has a beautiful physical resolution: the static coordinate description is not merely a mathematical curiosity or an artifact of coordinate choice—it accurately describes the operational, observationally-accessible reality that will confront any observer in the asymptotic future. Once the Hubble expansion becomes undetectable (because no external reference points remain to measure it against), the local patch of spacetime surrounding any surviving gravitationally-bound system will appear static, time-independent, and bounded by an impenetrable cosmological horizon—precisely the qualitative features of the static de Sitter coordinates.

# The ΛCDM Model and the Hubble Tension: Understanding Our Universe's Expansion

## The Standard Model of Cosmology

The Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model stands as the prevailing cosmological framework for understanding the universe's structure, composition, and evolution. This model incorporates three fundamental components: ordinary matter, cold dark matter (CDM), and dark energy—represented by the Greek letter Lambda (Λ), which corresponds to Einstein's cosmological constant.

According to ΛCDM, the universe consists of approximately 5% ordinary matter, 27% cold dark matter, and 68% dark energy. This composition explains numerous observational phenomena, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, the large-scale structure of galaxies, and the accelerating expansion of the universe. The model has proven remarkably successful at predicting and explaining a wide range of astronomical observations, making it the cornerstone of modern cosmology.

## The Hubble Constant

Central to the ΛCDM model is the Hubble constant (H₀), which measures the rate at which the universe is expanding. Named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, who first observed that galaxies are moving away from us at speeds proportional to their distance, this constant is typically expressed in kilometers per second per megaparsec (km/s/Mpc).

The Hubble constant serves as a critical parameter for determining the age, size, and ultimate fate of the universe. It also provides a bridge between theoretical predictions and observational astronomy, allowing scientists to calibrate distances across the cosmos.

## The Hubble Tension

In recent years, cosmologists have encountered a significant puzzle known as the "Hubble tension." This refers to a persistent discrepancy between two methods of measuring the Hubble constant:

**Early Universe Measurements**: Using data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), as measured by missions like the Planck satellite, combined with the ΛCDM model, scientists calculate a Hubble constant of approximately 67.4 km/s/Mpc.

**Local Universe Measurements**: Direct observations of nearby objects, such as Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae, yield a Hubble constant closer to 73 km/s/Mpc.

This discrepancy, now statistically significant at more than 5 sigma, cannot be easily dismissed as measurement error. The tension suggests either unknown systematic errors in one or both measurement methods, or—more intriguingly—that the ΛCDM model itself may be incomplete.

## Implications and Future Directions

The Hubble tension has profound implications for cosmology. Several theoretical solutions have been proposed, including:

- Modifications to dark energy's properties over cosmic time
- The existence of additional relativistic particles in the early universe
- New physics affecting the early universe before recombination
- Systematic errors in distance ladder calibrations

Upcoming missions and instruments, including the James Webb Space Telescope and various ground-based observatories, are providing increasingly precise measurements that may help resolve this tension. Some scientists view this discrepancy as an exciting opportunity—a potential crack in our current understanding that could lead to new physics beyond the standard ΛCDM model.

## Conclusion

The interplay between the ΛCDM model and the Hubble constant represents one of the most active and important areas of modern cosmological research. Whether the Hubble tension will be resolved through improved measurements or will require fundamental revisions to our cosmological model remains an open question. Either outcome promises to deepen our understanding of the universe's history, composition, and ultimate destiny.

# Cosmological Amnesia: The Fading Signatures of the Big Bang in an Accelerating Universe

## Abstract

The discovery of cosmic acceleration has profound implications not only for the future dynamics of the universe but for the very epistemology of cosmology itself. We examine how the ongoing accelerated expansion, driven by a cosmological constant, will progressively erase the observational signatures upon which our current understanding of the Big Bang model rests. As the universe continues to expand exponentially, three pillars of observational cosmology will become inaccessible to future observers: the cosmic microwave background will redshift into obscurity, with its photon density diluting below detectability within approximately 10^12 years; recession velocities of all extragalactic objects will exceed the speed of light as they cross the de Sitter horizon, rendering distant galaxies unobservable; and the light elements produced during Big Bang nucleosynthesis will become observationally indistinguishable from those produced by stellar processes, erasing this independent evidence for a hot early universe. We show that an observer in this far future—situated in an isolated, gravitationally bound galaxy (the merger product of the Local Group) embedded in an otherwise empty de Sitter space—would find no direct observational evidence for the expansion of the universe, the existence of other galaxies, or the thermal history of the cosmos. Such an observer, despite possessing potentially superior technology and scientific sophistication, would be led to conclude that they inhabit a static, eternal universe containing only their own galaxy, with no means of empirically verifying the Big Bang paradigm that stands as well-established in contemporary cosmology. We quantify the timescales over which each observational signature disappears and discuss the philosophical implications of this "cosmological horizon problem in time," arguing that the current era represents a uniquely privileged epoch for empirical cosmology—one in which the evidence for our cosmological origins remains observable, but which is destined to vanish irrevocably. These results underscore the contingent and time-dependent nature of scientific knowledge and suggest that future civilizations, however advanced, may face fundamental and insurmountable limits on their ability to reconstruct the history of the universe from observation alone.

# The "End of Cosmology" Hypothesis

This hypothesis, notably articulated by physicists including Lawrence Krauss and Robert Scherrer, argues that the accelerating expansion of the universe (driven by dark energy) will progressively erase the observational evidence that allows us to reconstruct cosmological history. Far-future observers—say, in ~100 billion years—will live in a universe that looks fundamentally different and will draw very different (and incomplete) conclusions about cosmology.

## The Core Mechanism: Accelerated Expansion

In a universe dominated by a cosmological constant (dark energy), space expands exponentially. This drives all gravitationally unbound galaxies beyond the cosmic horizon—the boundary beyond which light can never reach us, even given infinite time. Eventually, only a single gravitationally bound structure (the merged remnant of our Local Group) remains observable, sitting alone in an otherwise empty-looking universe.

## Loss of Key Evidence

**1. The Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)**
As the universe expands, the CMB photons redshift further and further, stretching their wavelength and diluting their number density. Eventually:
- The CMB's wavelength becomes longer than the observable horizon itself
- Its energy density drops below that of other foreground sources (e.g., free electrons in the interstellar/intergalactic medium, which produce their own faint plasma emission)
- The signal becomes fundamentally undetectable—not just faint, but masked by other emission and stretched beyond meaningful observation

Future astronomers would have no direct radiation signature of the hot Big Bang.

**2. Hubble Expansion**
Today we detect expansion by observing distant galaxies receding via redshift. In the far future:
- All other galaxies will have receded beyond the horizon
- The only remaining visible structure (the merged Local Group) will be a single, static, gravitationally bound galaxy
- With no external reference points, there will be no way to measure a Hubble law, no redshift-distance relation, and no observational signature of universal expansion at all

The universe will *appear* static, isolated, and unchanging—resembling a "island universe" model more than an expanding cosmos.

**3. Evidence of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN)**
The primordial abundances of light elements (hydrogen, helium, lithium) that currently serve as strong evidence for the hot Big Bang will still exist in some sense, but:
- Successive generations of star formation and death will process and reprocess this material
- Stellar nucleosynthesis will overwrite and contaminate primordial abundances with fusion/supernova products
- Distinguishing the *primordial* ratios from those produced by billions of years of stellar activity becomes practically impossible

## Philosophical Implication

The hypothesis carries a sobering epistemological lesson: **we may be living during a uniquely privileged era for observational cosmology.** Today we can see distant galaxies, measure the CMB, and infer BBN abundances precisely because we exist early enough in cosmic history, before accelerating expansion erases this evidence. Future civilizations, lacking our data, might reasonably (but incorrectly) conclude they inhabit a small, static, eternal universe—unable to reconstruct the Big Bang model at all.

This raises the unsettling possibility that *our own* cosmological models could be missing crucial data that was similarly erased before our era began, meaning our current picture of the universe might already be incomplete in ways we cannot detect.

This work examines the long-term evolution of ΛCDM cosmology under the extrapolation of accelerated expansion driven by a positive cosmological constant, demonstrating that the universe asymptotically approaches a de Sitter state characterized by exponential expansion, vanishing matter and radiation density, and a static, horizon-dominated causal structure. As the scale factor grows exponentially, comoving volumes are diluted to the point that all gravitationally unbound structures—galaxies, clusters, and eventually even the local group—recede beyond the cosmological event horizon, rendering them causally disconnected from any future observer. We show that within a timescale on the order of ~10¹² years, the observable universe will contain only a single gravitationally bound galactic remnant embedded in an empty, exponentially expanding background, with the cosmic microwave background redshifted beyond detectability and all relic radiation diluted below any measurable threshold. Consequently, future observers—if any persist—would find themselves in an apparently static, homogeneous, matter-free spacetime indistinguishable from empty de Sitter space, retaining no direct observational evidence of the Big Bang, primordial nucleosynthesis, the CMB, or large-scale structure formation. We formalize this "cosmological horizon problem in reverse," discuss its implications for the epistemic limits of future cosmology, and situate it within the broader context of the *Boltzmann brain* problem, the *end of cosmology* thesis, and the thermodynamics of de Sitter horizons. We argue that this asymptotic erasure of cosmological information imposes a fundamental constraint on the falsifiability and reconstructability of cosmological models over sufficiently long timescales, suggesting that empirical cosmology may be a historically contingent and temporally limited scientific enterprise. # The Epistemic Horizon of Future Cosmology: Observational Limits in an Accelerating Universe

## Introduction

The standard ΛCDM model describes a universe undergoing accelerated expansion driven by dark energy, with an exponential de Sitter phase asymptotically dominating the dynamics. While this model is empirically well-supported by contemporary observations—the cosmic microwave background (CMB), light element abundances from Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), and the large-scale distribution of galaxies—a striking consequence of continued accelerated expansion is that the very observational pillars supporting this cosmological model will become permanently inaccessible to observers in the far future. This raises a profound epistemological question: will future civilizations be able to reconstruct the correct cosmological history, or will the accelerating expansion erase the evidentiary basis for our current understanding? The consensus among cosmologists (following seminal work by Krauss and Scherrer, and Loeb) is that the answer is troubling: key observational signatures will vanish, rendering the inference of dark energy and the hot Big Bang increasingly difficult or impossible.

## The Recession of Extragalactic Structure

The fundamental mechanism underlying this loss of information is the exponential expansion characteristic of a universe dominated by a cosmological constant. In such a de Sitter phase, the Hubble parameter approaches a constant value, and all objects not gravitationally bound to the Local Group are carried beyond the cosmological event horizon. The proper distance to any given comoving galaxy grows exponentially with time, meaning that its recession velocity eventually exceeds the speed of light in the sense relevant to cosmological horizons. Consequently, over a timescale on the order of $10^{2}$ Gyr, all galaxies outside the Local Group (or Local Group remnant, following its eventual merger) will redshift beyond detectability and ultimately cross the de Sitter horizon.

This has direct consequences for the inference of dark energy itself. The discovery of cosmic acceleration relied on observations of Type Ia supernovae at cosmological distances, exploiting the *comparison* between the luminosity distances of nearby and distant standard candles to reveal the deviation from a matter-dominated deceleration. Once all extragalactic objects have receded beyond observable range, there will be no distant standard candles, no Hubble diagram, and no possibility of detecting the redshift-distance relation that originally revealed the accelerating expansion. Isolated observers within a single bound galactic remnant cannot detect Hubble expansion at all, since Hubble's law requires observation of multiple objects at varying distances undergoing systematic recession—a diagnostic that vanishes when only one bound structure remains observable.

## The Dilution and Redshifting of the Cosmic Microwave Background

The CMB constitutes the most direct relic evidence of the hot Big Bang, encoding the physics of recombination at $z \approx 1100$. However, in a perpetually expanding universe, the CMB temperature redshifts as $T \propto a^{-1}$, where $a$ is the scale factor. Under continued exponential expansion, the scale factor grows without bound, driving the CMB temperature asymptotically toward zero.

Crucially, this dilution does not proceed in isolation: the energy density of the CMB photons decreases as $\rho_{\rm CMB} \propto a^{-4}$, which falls precipitously faster than the (asymptotically constant) dark energy density. Within a timescale of order $10^{12}$ years, the CMB photon wavelength will be redshifted to scales exceeding the de Sitter horizon itself, and the photon number density will become so vanishingly small that, on average, less than a single CMB photon remains within the observable universe at any given time. At this point the CMB ceases to exist as a detectable radiation background in any meaningful statistical sense; it is not merely difficult to observe but physically absent as a measurable signal. Any future observer, regardless of technological sophistication, would find no thermal relic radiation to analyze, and hence no direct empirical access to the recombination epoch or the hot, dense early universe it implies.

## The Erasure of Primordial Nucleosynthesis Signatures

The third pillar, BBN, presents a subtler but equally severe problem. The primordial abundances of light elements (particularly the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio, and to a lesser extent helium-4 and lithium-7) serve as sensitive probes of the baryon-to-photon ratio and the physical conditions during the first few minutes after the Big Bang. These abundances are inferred today from observations of metal-poor astrophysical environments—high-redshift quasar absorption systems and metal-poor stars—that preserve primordial or near-primordial abundance ratios uncontaminated by stellar nucleosynthetic processing.

In the far future, however, continued star formation, stellar evolution, and interstellar recycling will progressively convert primordial hydrogen and deuterium into helium and heavier elements, while supernovae and stellar winds enrich the interstellar medium with metals. Deuterium, in particular, is fragile and only destroyed (not produced) in stellar interiors, so its primordial abundance will be progressively diluted and eventually erased as gas cycles through generations of stars. Once all matter in the Local Group remnant has been processed through multiple stellar generations, no pristine reservoirs of primordial-abundance gas will remain. Even if isolated pockets survived, the recession of all other galaxies beyond the horizon (as discussed above) would eliminate the observational baseline of diverse environments necessary to disentangle primordial abundances from the effects of chemical evolution—a task already highly dependent on comparative analysis across many independent systems.

## Epistemological Implications: The Problem of Cosmic Confirmation

The convergence of these three effects—the loss of the Hubble diagram, the dilution of the CMB below detectability, and the chemical processing of primordial light elements—implies that a civilization arising in the far future (say, $10^{12}$ years hence) within the isolated remnant of the Local Group would lack access to *any* of the primary empirical pillars upon which contemporary cosmology rests. Such observers would inhabit a universe that is, to all direct observational appearances, static, eternal, and unchanging: a single island of stars with no discernible external reference frame, no thermal background radiation, and no untouched primordial material.

This scenario illustrates a deep and somewhat unsettling point about the contingency of scientific knowledge: the correctness of a cosmological model may depend not only on the underlying physical reality but also on the *epoch* at which observers happen to exist relative to the timescales of cosmic structural and radiative evolution. It suggests that our current epoch may be cosmologically privileged in an observational sense—a "golden age" of cosmology—during which the relevant evidence remains accessible, in contrast to both the distant past (when structures had not yet formed) and the distant future (when the relevant relics will have been erased or removed from causal contact). This raises the broader methodological question of whether current cosmological models, however well-supported by present data, might themselves be incomplete reconstructions of a history whose full observational record is available only within a finite cosmic window—and correspondingly, whether future scientists, working from a diminished evidentiary base, could ever recover a correct cosmological picture through unaided empirical inference alone, absent inherited records from earlier epochs.

# Research Summary: Cosmological Recurrence to a Static de Sitter Framework

## Overview

This summary outlines a speculative but internally coherent cosmological argument: that the accelerating expansion driven by dark energy is not a transient phase toward a "heat death" of ever-increasing entropy and dilution, but rather an asymptotic *return* to the static, timeless geometry originally described by Willem de Sitter in 1917 — before Lemaître and others recast de Sitter space in expanding coordinates.

## Core Argument

**1. Observational trajectory.** Current data (SNe Ia, CMB, BAO) are consistent with a cosmological constant Λ dominating the energy budget. Under ΛCDM, as matter and radiation densities dilute, the universe asymptotically approaches pure de Sitter space — vacuum energy with no other stress-energy content.

**2. Coordinate reinterpretation.** Pure de Sitter space is a maximally symmetric solution admitting multiple coordinate representations. The **flat/expanding slicing** (FLRW-like, used since Friedmann–Lemaître) only covers half of the full de Sitter manifold and imposes a time-asymmetric, expansion-centric description. The **static patch** (de Sitter's original 1917 form) instead exhibits:
- A timelike Killing vector field (true stationarity)
- A cosmological horizon at fixed proper radius
- No global expansion — spatial geometry is static within the horizon

We argue that as ΛCDM evolution proceeds, the *physically relevant description* for any bound observer converges on the static patch, since:
- All matter/radiation redshifts away, leaving only vacuum energy
- Any comoving observer becomes causally isolated by the de Sitter horizon
- The residual physics (horizon thermodynamics, Gibbons–Hawking temperature) is naturally static-patch physics, not expansion physics

**3. Thermodynamic argument.** The Gibbons-Hawking temperature and horizon entropy are defined *in the static frame*. If the long-term equilibrium state of the universe is thermal (a de Sitter horizon in Unruh-like equilibrium with a single temperature $T_{dS} = H/2\pi$), then the natural late-time description is not one of continued "expansion" (which becomes operationally meaningless once no clocks, rulers, or comoving observers with distinguishable worldlines remain) but a **static, time-translation-invariant equilibrium** — which is precisely the original de Sitter static coordinate system.

**4. Loss of operational meaning for "expansion."** Once all observers are casually disconnected beyond the horizon and no dynamical matter remains to mark epochs, the scale factor $a(t)$ ceases to correspond to any measurable process. The residual description is a static, horizon-bounded patch with timeless (Killing-symmetric) geometry — expansion becomes a coordinate artifact of the earlier matter-dominated bookkeeping, not a physical feature of the terminal state.

## Implications

- The "expanding universe" may be best understood as a **transient coordinate description valid only while inhomogeneities/matter exist**, not a permanent ontological feature of spacetime.
- The terminal state of cosmological evolution is arguably better modeled as timeless and static, consistent with the *original* (pre-Lemaître) de Sitter solution.
- This reframes the arrow of cosmic time as an emergent, matter-dependent phenomenon rather than fundamental.

## Caveats

This remains a heterodox interpretation. It requires accepting that coordinate choice carries physical/ontological weight (a contested position), and it does not resolve why the universe began in the expanding patch rather than manifesting the static patch from the start. It should be regarded as a conceptual/interpretational proposal rather than a new dynamical prediction distinguishable from standard ΛCDM.
